newsitem.title: FRANCE: French markets on roll despite worst-case scenario.
newsitem.headline: French markets on roll despite worst-case scenario.

text.p: Defying all predictions, French financial assets have been on a roll since last Sunday's parliamentary election vaulted the Socialists to power, despite the party's market-unfriendly campaign promises.
Not even what economists called the "worst-case" outcome -- Communists joining the government to give the Socialists a majority -- has marred the honeymoon.

The blue-chip CAC-40 index of 40 leading stocks closed up 2.11 percent at 2,690.85 on Thursday, a gain of 165 points since the election. Bonds have also risen while the franc has firmed more than three-quarters of a centime against the mark.

Partly fuelling the markets has been a belief economic globalisation and the European Union's drive to forge a common currency mean policies will not change much from those of the ousted conservative government.
But some economists say it would be a mistake not to believe the Socialists, mindful of how ruthlessly voters turned on the conservatives, will not honour at least part of their platform.
"The French have voted for a left-wing coalition after they voted for a right-wing coalition which broke all its pledges," said Bernard Godement of financial house Daiwa.
"One thing ought to be clear. If they do not want to lose power, they will have to implement some of their policies."
"The government faces strong pressure to apply what it has been announcing," said Philippe Brossard of ABN-Amro Finance. "Otherwise, unions, public opinion will react very strongly."
Markets have been "a bit too sanguine" in assuming the new government will pursue centrist policies, Brossard said.

New finance and industry minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn is a "pragmatist," said Brossard. But he will apply a "much more left-wing policy than (former Socialist prime minister Pierre) Beregevoy...The context is not centre-left, it is left wing."

During the campaign, the Socialists pledged to put economic growth and jobs at the top of the political agenda to counter a record 12.8 percent unemployment rate. They said they would create 700,000 jobs, half of them in the public sector, and cut France's work week to 35 hours from 39 over five years.
They also pledged to halt privatisations, boost wages, make it harder to fire workers and opposed recent legislation to introduce private pension funds.
While supporting European monetary union, Prime Minister Lionel Jospin said he was against a new bout of austerity to fulfill the strict deficit conditions to qualify.

Not all this bodes ill for financial markets. With the possibility of growth and job-priming measures, "stocks are safe, at least cyclical ones or very consumer oriented," said Brossard. "Also any stock exposed to the dollar."

"We've suddenly discovered the virtues of the Socialists which the market considered lower than the ground before the runoff vote -- the scenario of a weak euro," said Hugues de Montvallon, economist at Paris brokerage Oddo.
Retailers, such as Carrefour and Promodes have all done well in the last few days.
But banks and manufacturing industry have been hit by plans by the Socialists to make it more difficult to fire employees.
Defence stocks have been gouged by the Socialists' pledge to halt any privatisations including those of electronics group Thomson-CSF .
Key to the bond market's performance will be how quickly the Socialists introduce job creation measures and push up wages.

"It's important from a budget point of view in the context of the Maastricht treaty (on monetary union) that they don't try to create too many jobs and load up the public sector cost," said bond analyst Iain Lindsay of Credit Lyonnais.
"We still don't know yet what Jospin had to give to the Communists to get their participation in government," he said.
Also vital will be France's position, due to be announced on Monday, on the stability pact designed to police budget deficits after introduction of a single currency.
Jospin said during the campaign he wanted to renegotiate the pact, slated to be ratified in Amsterdam in mid-June.
"He was quite adamant he did not feel obliged to accept the stability pact," said Lindsay. "This will be the first measure of how strenuous his word is."
